title: Two words in one
goal: Hear both meanings of a homonym, and read the cinas of a mani and the sounds of a tongue twister.

intro.text: Many short Turkish nouns have a verb twin, because the imperative is the bare stem: *yüz* (face) and *Yüz!* (Swim!). Folk poets rhyme on such pairs (*cinas*), and tongue twisters (*yanıltmaç*) pile up sounds that sit close together in the mouth.

vocab.en: hail (dolu yağmak: to hail); also full
stream, brook (a homonym of çay, tea)
a play on homonyms, especially in a rhyme
rhymed formula of a tale or a game; tongue twister

exercises.question: A father shouts *Yüz!* to his son at the edge of a pool. What does he mean?

why.1: *Yüz* is also a face, but nobody shouts a face at a swimmer.
why.2: The number makes no sense as a shout by a pool.
why.3: **Laugh!** is *Gül!*, another bare stem with a noun twin (rose).

exercises.explain: The second-person imperative is the bare stem: *yüzmek* → *Yüz!*. That is why so many short nouns have a verb twin.

exercises.question: Which reading of *yazın* fits this sentence: *Tatilde bana bol bol mektup yazın.*?

why.1: The time is already given, *tatilde*, and *mektup* needs a verb.
why.2: **Your summer** would leave the sentence without a verb.
why.3: A genitive would need a possessed noun after it.

exercises.explain: *yaz-* + `-(y)In`: the polite or plural imperative, like *okuyun*. The same letters also spell *yazın*, in summer.

exercises.en: When she saw the roses in the garden, she laughed.

accept: gülleri

reject.why: *Görmek* takes a definite object in the accusative: *gülleri*.

accept: güldü

reject.why: *Gülümsemek* is to smile. The sentence wants the twin of *gül*: *güldü*.

exercises.hint: Both blanks begin with the same three letters.
exercises.explain: *gül* + *-ler* + *-i* (the roses, as an object) and *gül-* + `-DI` (she laughed): one sound, two words.

accept: When it hailed, all the cafés were full.
When it hailed, all the cafes were full
When it hailed, all the coffee shops were full
When it started hailing, [all the cafés|all the cafes|all the coffee shops] were full
When it started to hail, [all the cafés|all the cafes|all the coffee shops] were full
When it began hailing, [all the cafés|all the cafes|all the coffee shops] were full
When it began to hail, [all the cafés|all the cafes|all the coffee shops] were full
When it [hailed|started hailing|started to hail|began hailing|began to hail], [every café|every cafe|every coffee shop] was full
When it [hailed|started hailing|started to hail|began hailing|began to hail], the [cafés|cafes|coffee shops] were all full
When the hail [came|started|began], [all the cafés|all the cafes|all the coffee shops] were full
When the hail [came|started|began], [every café|every cafe|every coffee shop] was full
[All the cafés|All the cafes|All the coffee shops] were full when it [hailed|started hailing|started to hail]
[Every café|Every cafe|Every coffee shop] was full when it [hailed|started hailing|started to hail]
exercises.explain: The first *dolu* is a noun, hail, the subject of *yağmak*; the second, with the past copula, is the adjective **full**.

exercises.tr: Dal sarkar kartal kalkar, kartal kalkar dal sarkar.
exercises.en: The branch droops and the eagle takes off; the eagle takes off and the branch droops.
options: Dal sarkar kartal kalkar, kartal kalkar dal sarkar.
Dal sarkar kartal kalkar, kartal sarkar dal kalkar.
Kartal kalkar dal sarkar, dal kalkar kartal sarkar.

exercises.question: In this kesik mani, what are the two *bağlar* at the end of lines 2 and 4?

context.tr: Böyle bağlar / Yâr başın böyle bağlar / Gül açmaz bülbül ötmez / Yıkılsın böyle bağlar

why.1: Line 2 has a subject, *yâr*, and an object, *başın* (her head): it needs a verb.
why.2: Then there would be no cinas: the rhyme word must change its meaning.
why.3: Line 2 needs a verb, and the rhyme would lose its pun.

exercises.explain: *bağla-* + `-r`, the aorist (she ties), and *bağ* + *-lar*, vineyards: the same sounds, two words. Line 4 wishes ruin on gardens where no rose blooms.

exercises.prompt: In summer, write to me every day.
accept: Yazın bana her gün yaz.
Yazın bana her gün yazın
Yazın bana her gün yazınız
Yazın her gün bana [yaz|yazın|yazınız]
Yaz boyunca bana her gün [yaz|yazın|yazınız]
Yaz boyunca her gün bana [yaz|yazın|yazınız]
Yazın bana her gün mektup [yaz|yazın]

reject.why: For **in summer** Turkish uses the adverb *yazın*, as *kışın* for **in winter**.

exercises.explain: With *siz* the sentence says the same word twice in two meanings: *Yazın* (in summer) … *yazın* (write!).

exercises.task: Write two Turkish sentences, each using one of these homonyms in both its meanings: *yüz*, *gül*, *at* or *dolu*.
models: Havuza girmeden önce yüzünü yıkadı, sonra yarım saat yüzdü. Bahçede güller açınca annem çok güldü.
Çocuk atın önüne bir elma attı. Dolu yağarken bütün kafeler doluydu.
checklist: Each sentence uses one word in two unrelated meanings
The verb twin is a real form of *yüzmek*, *gülmek* or *atmak*
The noun has the case it needs: *yüzünü*, *gülleri*, *atın önüne*
Optional: put the second meaning last, so the pun lands at the end

exercises.en: When he saw the horse, he threw the ball.
